atlanta.intro: Trees Atlanta keeps a list of the city's biggest trees, and its champions turn up in odd places, beside the drive to a tennis centre, on the pavement outside the High Museum, leaning over the BeltLine path, in a private yard in Poncey-Highland. These eleven trees come from that list. The tallest, a tulip tree in Atlanta Memorial Park, was measured at 50.6 metres. The oldest by its own account is the Grandfather Beech in southwest Atlanta, which Atlanta Magazine dates to 1863. Most are free to see.
atlanta.meta_description: Atlanta's champion trees, from a 50.6-metre tulip tree by a tennis centre to the Grandfather Beech and the ginkgo outside the High Museum.
atlanta.question_meta: The oldest tree on Atlanta's list is the Grandfather Beech, dated to 1863 by Atlanta Magazine. An Oakland Cemetery magnolia dates from after the Civil War.
atlanta.question_answer: The oldest tree on this Atlanta list is the Grandfather Beech at the Outdoor Activity Center in southwest Atlanta, which Atlanta Magazine dates to 1863, about 160 years ago, though it gives no basis for the year. Close behind is a southern magnolia in Oakland Cemetery that a Confederate soldier's brother planted after the Civil War, and which now holds up the soldier's leaning gravestone. Most of the city's other champion trees have never been dated.
atlanta.question_context: Atlanta's big trees are measured far more often than they are dated. The Trees Atlanta champion program records girth, height and crown for the largest tree of each species in the city, and almost none of those records carries an age. What the city does have is old ground. Herbert Taylor and Daniel Johnson parks in Morningside hold a remnant of the hickory and beech forest that stood there when the Muscogee (Creek) ceded the land in the 1820s, with some trees put at 150 to 180 years old or more. Fernbank Forest in Druid Hills, 65 acres of old growth bought by local citizens in 1939, has tulip poplars and white oaks on one slope reaching about 156 feet. The Outdoor Activity Center in southwest Atlanta keeps another remnant, and the Grandfather Beech inside it, dated by Atlanta Magazine to 1863. In Oakland Cemetery, a magnolia planted after the Civil War grows against a soldier's grave. The tallest measured tree on this list, a tulip tree beside the Bitsy Grant Tennis Center, stands 50.6 metres and has no recorded age at all. If you know when any of these went in, tell us.

faq.q: Can you reach Atlanta's champion trees by MARTA?
faq.a: Some of them. The High Museum ginkgo is by the Woodruff Arts Center complex at Arts Center station, the Vine City elm is in the same neighbourhood as Vine City station, and King Memorial is the station closest to Oakland Cemetery. The trees in Herbert Taylor Park, Atlanta Memorial Park and Fernbank Forest are easier by car or bike.

faq.q: Do you need a ticket to see the trees?
faq.a: For nearly all of them, no. The parks, the BeltLine path along Tanyard Creek and the grounds of Oakland Cemetery are free, and the High Museum ginkgo stands by the public sidewalk, so no museum ticket is needed. Fernbank Forest is open daily until 4:30 pm; check with Fernbank Museum whether the forest needs a ticket. The Outdoor Activity Center lists no hours and closes on some Saturdays for events, so check before going.

faq.q: Can you visit the champion black tupelo in Poncey-Highland?
faq.a: Only from the street. It grows in a private yard at 622 Moreland Avenue NE and is clearly visible from the public sidewalk, which is where to stand. It is at its best in autumn colour.

great-smoky-mountains.intro: Three trees in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, all on the Tennessee side, and each takes some walking. The largest tulip tree in the park, by one count, stands with its top gone at the end of a three-mile climb to Albright Grove. Three old tulip poplars stand together about two and a half miles up the Ramsey Cascades Trail. In Cades Cove, a sweet gum planted on the day of the Pearl Harbor attack grows on a hillside behind a gravel pull-off. If you know other old trees in the park worth the walk, tell us.
great-smoky-mountains.meta_description: Old trees in the Great Smoky Mountains: the giant of Albright Grove, the Ramsey Cascades poplars and Cades Cove's Pearl Harbor Tree, with trail distances.
great-smoky-mountains.question_meta: Albright Grove's tulip tree, over 25 feet round, is a 6.5-mile round trip; the Ramsey Cascades poplars stand about 2.5 miles up their trail.
great-smoky-mountains.question_answer: Two trails lead to the biggest trees on this list. The Maddron Bald Trail near Cosby climbs about 2.9 miles to the Albright Grove Loop, where a tulip tree a little over 25 feet round, which smokymountains.com calls the largest in the park, stands at the end of a short signed spur; the National Park Service gives 6.5 miles round trip. The Ramsey Cascades Trail in Greenbrier passes three big tulip poplars about two and a half miles up, the largest at least seven feet across.
great-smoky-mountains.question_context: Big trees in the Smokies are a walk away, and the walks change. Albright Grove is old forest on the Tennessee side in the Cosby area, and several of its giants have died, including a huge snag and a stump that earlier visitors recorded. The tulip tree still called the king of the grove lost its crown, possibly to lightning, and was measured at 25 feet 3 inches round in 2019, the latest published account of it. The Ramsey Cascades Trail was damaged by floods in 2022 and again in 2024, and the park reopened it full-time in 2024 after a three-year restoration; its three poplars were last described in January 2024. In Cades Cove the story is human. Golman Myers planted a sweet gum in his front yard when news of Pearl Harbor reached the cove in December 1941, and in 2022 the park brought Medal of Honor recipients to see it. None of these trees has a published age except that one. Before you drive out, check the park's alerts for trail and road closures, and if you have stood under any of them lately, tell us how they are.

faq.q: Do you need to pay to see these trees?
faq.a: There is no entrance fee for Great Smoky Mountains National Park, and the trails are free to walk. Any vehicle parked for longer than 15 minutes needs a Park It Forward parking tag, at 5 dollars a day, 15 a week or 40 a year, except on the park's free entrance days.

faq.q: How long is the hike to Albright Grove?
faq.a: The National Park Service gives 6.5 miles (10.5 km) round trip from the Maddron Bald Trailhead at the end of Baxter Road, including the 0.7-mile loop through the grove, with about 1,475 feet of climbing on a moderate to steep, rough trail. Parking at the trailhead is limited.

faq.q: Can you get to the trees without a car?
faq.a: No. There is no public transport to any of the three, and no shuttle to the trailheads. Ramsey Prong Road is partly gravel and the Cades Cove Loop Road is one-way and closed to cars on some mornings in season, so check the park's road status before you go.

chattanooga.intro: A willow oak at Bonny Oaks, on the north-east side of Chattanooga, was already standing when an orphanage opened on the farm around it in 1854, by the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council's account. It grows in a small round arboretum of 55 species in front of the Dent House, built in 1840, and the arboretum is free and open every day, about 10 miles from downtown. If you know another old tree in Chattanooga worth the walk, tell us.
chattanooga.meta_description: The Bonny Oaks Willow Oak in Chattanooga, a registered Historic Tree said to predate the 1854 Bonny Oaks Orphanage, in a free arboretum.
chattanooga.question_meta: The Bonny Oaks Willow Oak predates the 1854 Bonny Oaks Orphanage, says the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council, which makes it over 170 years old.
chattanooga.question_answer: The Bonny Oaks Willow Oak stands in Bonny Oaks Arboretum at 6183 Adamson Circle, in front of the Dent House on the north-east side of Chattanooga. The Tennessee Urban Forestry Council says it dates from before 1854, which would make it more than 170 years old; Wikipedia says over 100 years and calls it the oldest tree in the arboretum.
chattanooga.question_context: The willow oak at Bonny Oaks has outlasted several owners of the ground it stands on. This was Cherokee land before Colonel Lewis Shepherd settled the area. Colonel Jarrett G. Dent built his house there in 1840, and the Dent House is now on the National Register of Historic Places and serves as the Hamilton County Agriculture Center. In 1854 the Bonny Oaks Orphanage was established on the farm to teach children agricultural skills, and the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council says the willow oak was already growing by then. In 1867 Captain C. C. Peak named the place Bonnie Oaks for the stately oaks around the homestead. The council listed the tree as a Historic Tree in 2000. Sources disagree on its age, from over 100 years in Wikipedia to over 170 by the council's account, and nobody has published its girth or height. The arboretum around it holds 55 species in a small round park on county land, free and open daily. If you go with a tape measure, tell us what you find.

faq.q: Is Bonny Oaks Arboretum free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It is a small round park on Hamilton County Parks land, open daily without charge, in front of the Dent House at 6183 Adamson Circle.

faq.q: How far is the Bonny Oaks Willow Oak from downtown Chattanooga?
faq.a: About 10 miles, on the north-east side of the city near Lake Vista.
